passage: Across diverse cultures, rhythmic music and synchronized movement have long served as powerful tools for forging social cohesion. Whether through communal drumming, religious chanting, or group dance, moving together in time blurs the psychological boundaries between self and others. Anthropologists and neuroscientists suggest that synchronous activity triggers the release of endorphins, which elevate pain thresholds and foster feelings of trust and warmth toward fellow participants. Remarkably, even brief periods of coordinated action—such as marching in step or singing in unison—can make strangers more willing to cooperate and share resources afterward. Long before modern institutions or legal contracts existed, shared rhythm functioned as an evolutionary glue that enabled large human groups to coordinate efforts, resolve conflicts, and thrive collectively.
